memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text:
"'An uncle or a cousin or any blood relative in their clan may redeem them.
Or if they prosper, they may redeem themselves. They and their buyer are to
count the time from the year they sold themselves up to the Year of Jubilee'"
- Lev 25:49-50 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
God spells out who could redeem the fallen person: an uncle, a cousin, any
blood relative. The circle of possible redeemers was wide. Someone in the
family had both the right and the opportunity to step in and pay the price.

The one condition running through all of it is kinship. The redeemer had to
be a relative — connected by blood, near enough to have the right to act.
This was not a stranger's charity; it was family responsibility. The bond of
kinship gave both the right and the obligation to rescue.

Dear friend, this is exactly why the Son of God became one of us. To be our
Redeemer, He had to become our relative. And so the eternal Word took on
flesh and blood. Hebrews says that since the children have flesh and blood, He
too shared in their humanity, so that by His death He might set them free
(Heb 2:14-15).

He was not ashamed to call us brothers and sisters (Heb 2:11). He became our
near kinsman precisely so that He could redeem us. The incarnation was not an
optional extra; it was essential to our rescue. Only a true relative could
buy us back.

When you look at the manger, you are looking at the beginning of your
redemption. God became near enough to save you.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Do I marvel that God became my relative in order to redeem me?
2. What does the incarnation reveal about the lengths of God's love?
3. How does being redeemed by a kinsman deepen my sense of belonging to God?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text:
Lord Jesus, You took on flesh and blood to become my near kinsman and my
Redeemer. Thank You for the wonder of coming close enough to save me. Amen.
